Chapter 6: Welcoming Abundance and Rewriting the Money Story
Let’s talk about money. Just saying the word can bring up a swirl of emotions—hope, fear, maybe even a little envy or shame. For most of us, money isn’t just about dollars and cents. It’s tangled up with feelings about self-worth, safety, and what’s possible in life.
Think about the stories you grew up with. Maybe you heard, “money doesn’t grow on trees.” Every spending decision felt heavy. Bills might have brought a pit in your stomach. And as you got older, did you notice those patterns showing up again? Maybe you hesitated to invest in yourself, or felt guilty for wanting a bit more, or even resented those who seemed to have it easier. When an opportunity knocked, did a little voice whisper, “You don’t deserve this,” or “It’s selfish to want more”?
Here’s something to really consider: most of us don’t realize just how much our relationship with money is inherited. The beliefs you picked up as a kid—about what’s possible, what’s fair, and what’s safe—can quietly become the script for your adult life. For some, money is a source of conflict. For others, it’s tied to success or even love. These old money stories shape everything: your career choices, your spending habits, and even your dreams.
But there comes a moment when you start to question those old scripts. Maybe it’s a moment of frustration—working hard, but feeling like you’re never getting ahead. Or maybe it’s a flash of envy, watching someone else take a risk and win. And suddenly, you realize the real limits aren’t in your paycheck—they’re in the beliefs you’ve carried about what’s possible.
So, how do we start changing the money story? The first step is awareness. Next time a bill arrives, notice your first reaction. Is it dread? Gratitude? Maybe indifference? When a new opportunity pops up, do you reach for it, or do you shrink back? Most people don’t even realize how quickly they talk themselves out of abundance.
Let me share a story with you. Someone spent years just scraping by—always anxious about money. Then, they decided to look at money differently. Instead of seeing it as a source of stress, they started to see it as a tool—a way to create, give, and experience life more fully. They celebrated every bit of income, no matter how small. And gradually, that shift in attitude opened new doors. Unexpected opportunities showed up, new clients appeared, and that heavy sense of scarcity slowly faded away.
And here’s a big piece of the puzzle: gratitude. By paying attention to what you already have and truly appreciating it, you’ll find it much easier to welcome more. This isn’t about ignoring your challenges—it’s about balancing them with appreciation for what’s working. Over time, this habit actually rewires your mind to look for abundance, making it easier to spot opportunities and take action.
Generosity matters, too. It’s easy to hold onto money tightly, worried that giving will leave you with less. But the act of giving—whether it’s your time, your energy, or your resources—creates a sense of flow. It reminds you that there’s enough to go around, and abundance actually grows when it’s shared.
One last thing: forgiving past mistakes is so important. A lot of people carry shame about debt, missed chances, or financial missteps. But holding onto guilt only keeps that old story alive. When you forgive yourself, and choose to learn from those moments, you make space to move forward—with confidence and hope.
